summaries.Q1952944: Founded on 16 February 1798 by the drawing teacher Louis-Joseph Jay, the museum has occupied place de Lavalette since 1994, on the site of a Franciscan convent built in 1218. Its 57 permanent rooms range from ancient Egypt to contemporary art, from Matisse's Interior with Aubergines to Warhol's portrait of Jackie Kennedy.
summaries.Q3329695: Founded in 1906 at the initiative of the ethnographer Hippolyte Müller, it occupies the former Visitandine convent of Sainte-Marie d'en-Haut, on the first slopes of the Bastille. The museum was inaugurated there by André Malraux on 3 February 1968, during the Winter Olympic Games.
summaries.Q3329436: Beneath the former church of Saint-Laurent, deconsecrated in 1983, the buildings are stacked over a Gallo-Roman necropolis. The jewel of the site is the 6th-century crypt of Saint-Oyand, whose existence was revealed in 1803 by Jacques-Joseph Champollion, the elder brother of the Egyptologist. The place became a museum in 1986.
summaries.Q3330877: Founded in 1775 as a natural history cabinet promoted by Doctor Henri Gagnon, Stendhal's maternal grandfather, it opened its present building in 1855. In the neighbouring jardin des Plantes, a small artificial stream is crossed by the world's first structure in poured concrete, built in 1855 by Joseph and Louis Vicat.
summaries.Q3224155: This 3,000 m2 hall was built in Paris in 1900 by the workshops of Gustave Eiffel for the World's Fair, then dismantled and re-erected in Grenoble, where it served for sixty years as a boilermaking workshop before becoming a storage space. The national centre for contemporary art was inaugurated there on 26 April 1986.
summaries.Q2858640: After his mother's death, Stendhal lived here from 1790 to 1796 with his maternal grandfather, Doctor Henri Gagnon: two adjoining houses of the 16th and 17th centuries, one opening onto place Grenette, the other onto the jardin de ville. The flat served him as a laboratory for observing Grenoble's polite society.
summaries.Q22996666: Henri Beyle, known as Stendhal, was born on 23 January 1783 on the second floor of this house at 14, rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau, then called rue des Vieux-Jésuites, and lived there until the age of seven. The building, privately owned, housed the museum of the Dauphiné Resistance from 1966 to 1994.
summaries.Q2901456: It came into being in 1772 with the purchase by subscription of the library of Bishop Jean de Caulet, 33,644 works knocked down for 45,000 livres. It holds the collections of Champollion, Stendhal and Berlioz. Since 1970 its headquarters has occupied the former university library on boulevard Maréchal-Lyautey.
summaries.Q2994563: Born of a music school created in 1922 and made a municipal conservatoire in 1935, the institution left the former Minim convent in April 1969 for this building on chemin de Gordes, inaugurated on 27 June 1970 in the presence of the Minister of Culture Edmond Michelet. In 2025 it took the name of Nina Simone.
summaries.Q2942283: Built from the 10th century onwards, it has, in a very dense urban fabric, the peculiarity of having residential buildings abutting its structure and of communicating with the church of Saint-Hugues. In 1989 the tramway works uncovered its 4th-century baptistery, preserved in the archaeological crypt of the musée de l'Ancien Évêché.
summaries.Q2983944: Founded in 1228 as the private chapel of the dauphins, to house their tombs, it was built with the revenue from the silver mines of Brandes-en-Oisans. Its bell rang the sing at 10 every evening, warning the inhabitants that the city gates were about to close: the custom lasted until 1877.
summaries.Q16467688: Built from 1922 in a Romano-Byzantine style, to plans drawn up by the first parish priest, Father Joseph Viallet, son of the mayor Félix Viallet. Consecrated unfinished in 1943, it saw the works halt in 1969, and the planned 75-metre campanile was never erected.
summaries.Q2887006: The threshold of the first church of Saint-Joseph, consecrated in 1697 in a suburb outside the ramparts, served as the reference point for determining the exact altitude of Grenoble: 213.48 metres. The old church having been demolished, the present basilica was consecrated in 1924. Abbé Pierre was a curate there from 1939 to 1942.
summaries.Q3582365: Founded at the request of Bishop Le Camus of Grenoble, who consecrated it in 1699: he wanted two new parishes, Saint-Louis inside the city and Saint-Joseph outside the walls. Above the doorway, a Latin inscription recalls that Louis the Great had this house built for the Lord, in the year 1699. The organ installed in 1980 has 61 stops.
summaries.Q2385384: Built from 1963 to 1965 by the architect Maurice Blanc, a native of the city, it follows a circular plan 37 metres in diameter and can hold 1,300 people. Its self-supporting hyperboloid roof, rebuilt in 1979 after leaks, was completely reinterpreted. It has been listed as 20th-century heritage since 2003.
summaries.Q595256: In 1671 the Reverend Minim Fathers complained of being disturbed in their meditation by the singing coming from the Protestant temple close by: a royal ordinance had the temple moved beyond the ramparts. Their convent, built from 1644, today houses a student residence and a concert hall, named salle Olivier Messiaen in 1981.
summaries.Q101086115: Jewish worship in Grenoble is spread among several organisations. They include the consistorial synagogue Bar Yohaï, the religious association Zekhout Avot, which also houses a synagogue, the Lubavitch community, with a school and a mikveh, and the liberal Jewish community Beit ha Or.
summaries.Q545992: Sent to inspect the fortifications of the Alps in September 1692, Vauban mocked the stronghold: a winegrower was its governor, with twelve cows and eight goats, a mare and a donkey for the whole garrison. The fort visited today, begun in April 1824, took 23 years of work.
summaries.Q2446035: The first reinforced concrete tower built in the world, raised in 1924 by Auguste Perret for the International Exhibition of Hydroelectric Power. Its 84 metres to the last element of concrete owe nothing to chance: he wanted one metre more than the Sacré-Cœur in Montmartre, in tribute to his father, a Communard stonecutter.
summaries.Q3361193: Seat of the Parliament of Dauphiné, a sovereign court created in 1453 by Louis XI, then a courthouse until 2002. It was from its blue drawing room that the Day of the Tiles set out, on 7 June 1788, the first event of the Dauphiné revolution. A monk accused of witchcraft underwent 230 sessions of interrogation there before his conviction in 1606.
summaries.Q3533160: This square brick tower, dated 1350, is the remnant of a fortified house, today standing in the Olympic village district. It was first called the Vaulnaveys farm, after its first owner; it owes its present name to the nuns of the Chartreuse de Prémol, who bought it. It houses a children's centre.
summaries.Q22966989: In 1794 a plaque placed on this 17th-century mansion proclaimed that Jacques Vaucanson was born here on 24 February 1709. It was false: the creator of automata was born at 3, rue Brocherie, and moved in only in 1717, aged 8, as an ordinary tenant. The plaque has been removed, the name maison Vaucanson has remained.
summaries.Q22966991: Built against the Roman rampart from 1471 by the Rabot family, this mansion today houses the Arthaud bookshop. Charles VIII, Louis XII and Francis I stayed there; it was the first of them who authorised, in 1494, the piercing of the rampart to reach his garden, the origin of today's passage de la République.
summaries.Q1545706: Inaugurated on 29 September 1934, it is one of the first cable cars built in a large urban area, with 266 metres of vertical rise up to the Bastille. Its blue twelve-sided cabins were replaced as early as March 1951. The bubbles of the engineer Denis Creissels, designed so that everyone could see out, entered service on 31 July 1976.
summaries.Q3007086: Grenoble was first called Cularo, a Gaulish place name that probably meant “gourd field”. Its first written mention dates from 6 June 43 BC: a letter from the governor Lucius Munatius Plancus to Cicero. The town would take the name Gratianopolis in 381.
summaries.Q3076251: It commemorates the Grenoble summer of 1788, the Day of the Tiles and the meeting of the estates general of Dauphiné, bringing together in Carrara marble the Third Estate, the Clergy and the Nobility reconciled. Inaugurated on 4 August 1897 before President Félix Faure, nine years late: its sculptor, Henri Ding, was not even introduced to the head of state.
summaries.Q85854765: On 21 August 1822 the remains of the knight Bayard were transferred to the neighbouring collegiate church of Saint-André; the same day this statue by Nicolas Raggi, cast by Charles Crozatier, was unveiled. It shows Bayard wounded, leaning against a rock, raising to his lips the hilt of his sword, which suggests a cross.
summaries.Q3399041: Erected in 1620 by Lesdiguières as part of the fortification of the Bastille hill, it bears military trophies in bas-relief carved by Jacob Richier. Turner drew it in 1802 in his Grenoble Sketchbook. Since 1935 it has been the city's war memorial: 1,722 names for 1914-1926.
summaries.Q22966994: Raised in 1615 on the orders of Lesdiguières, it has kept its machicolation above the vaulted passage and two bretèches intended to defend the pedestrian doors. Until 1864, all the gates of Grenoble stayed closed from 10 at night to 7 in the morning, except this one, open from 5.
summaries.Q3140615: In a stairwell of the lycée, two small mirrors set on the window ledges throw onto the ceiling a patch of sunlight that runs across baroque frescoes: it gives the true solar time, the day, the month, the sign of the zodiac. The Jesuit father Jean Bonfa completed this reflection dial in 1673.
summaries.Q3272779: Inaugurated on 3 February 1968 by André Malraux thanks to the Olympic Games budget, the house of culture by André Wogenscky suggested to journalists a great white liner topped by two black volumes. Its mobile stage had a revolving platform on which the audience took their seats. Renamed Le Cargo in 1985, it has been the MC2 since 2004.
summaries.Q3363879: A former firing range of the engineer corps, this 21-hectare park owes its layout to the international exhibition of hydroelectric power, which drew 1,050,000 visitors in 1925. A zoological garden there kept two star bears, Martin and Michka, given by the Russian ambassador. The park has borne the name of the mayor Paul Mistral since 1932.
summaries.Q17000301: The sculpture park of the musée de Grenoble, it has brought together since 1988 some fifteen monumental 20th-century works, among them Conversation by George Rickey, whose steel arms are in permanent motion. It is also home to the oldest tree in the city, a cedar of Lebanon planted in 1847.
summaries.Q125660255: The first garden of the bishops' palace dates from 1775; the present one, L-shaped, was laid out in 2014. Its last section reveals the east end of the cathedral, a 13th-century brick chancel built on the crest of the Roman rampart, and a fortified wall-walk of 1374.
summaries.Q96380281: Since 2022 this botanical garden has borne the name of Joséphine Baker. In 1850 it displayed caged lions, including a Barbary lioness that died in 1856; in 2023 her taxidermied body was kept in the zoology store of the Muséum. Its little bridge, built in 1855 by Louis Vicat and his son Joseph, is one of the world's first in poured concrete.
summaries.Q113838764: At the end of the 18th century the merchant Jean-Baptiste Dolle bought this rock for 2,400 livres and had sumptuous gardens laid out there from 1787 to 1789, along with a house that the people of Grenoble nicknamed the Château de la Folie. With no spring on site, the water was pumped from the Isère. Under the Terror, Dolle handed the estate over to the Nation.
summaries.Q3397282: Built from 1956 to 1958 to replace a metal structure of 1893, this bridge owes its name to the monumental gate raised in 1620 when Lesdiguières fortified the city. It crosses the Isère at an angle, at 70 grads, to spare those arriving the former right-angle bend. Since 2019 it has also borne the name of Kofi Annan.
summaries.Q65126347: Opened on 7 February 1828 in place of an old cable ferry, the first bridge was suspended by chains, the work of the engineer Louis Crozet, a future mayor of Grenoble. Its arched successor, built in 1938, was sabotaged by German troops in August 1944, then partly swept away by the flood of 1954.
summaries.Q118470177: Opened to traffic around 1840, this quay was cut into a rock that once reached the Isère: only a narrow path, inherited from antiquity, led to the small harbour known as la Roche. After the discovery of a seam of cement stone by Louis Vicat in 1840, the cement works of mont Jalla settled along the quay.
summaries.Q3396916: Brought into service on 24 January 2011 after thirteen months of works, it replaces the temporary bridge put up in 2004 for the tramway project. Of its 17 metres of width, the roadway takes only 6: pavements and cycle lanes give priority to pedestrians and bicycles. Its name comes from the massif facing it.
summaries.Q85854375: Its name comes from the grain markets held there in the Middle Ages: the Granaterie, then the Grenette. At the far end of the square, the Lavalette water tower, brought into service in 1827, is adorned with four cherubs riding bronze dolphins, emblems of the Dauphiné.
summaries.Q62070763: Justice was dispensed at the palace of the Parliament of Dauphiné until 2002, hence the local nickname “place du Trib”. At the centre stands the statue of the knight Pierre Terrail de Bayard; on one side, the café de la Table ronde, the oldest café in Grenoble.
summaries.Q109018356: This square, 150 metres on each side, was first the place d'Armes, designed in the 1840s on the site of a bastion of the Lesdiguières fortifications; it took the name of Verdun in 1918. A statue of Napoleon I on horseback was unveiled there in 1868, dismantled in 1870, then re-erected near the lake of Laffrey.
summaries.Q118470279: The northern part of the square corresponds to the site of the porte Herculea, one of the two original gates of the Roman wall. The fontaine des Trois ordres, built from 1888, was inaugurated in 1897 during the official visit of the President of the Republic to Grenoble.
summaries.Q118470123: This small square courtyard, closed to car traffic, was called place du Cloître-Notre-Dame in the Middle Ages, then place des Tillots in 1694: the word is said to evoke the teillots, the hemp dressers. The present name was fixed by a resolution of the municipal council on 9 October 1857.
summaries.Q108936563: Opened in 1338, when the suburb had already grown up outside the walls, the street owes its name either to the term Trans-Claustra or to the three cloisters of the district. Bordered until the 19th century by the Verderet stream, it suffered many floods; a flood marker recalls that of November 1859.
summaries.Q106305111: Opened in 1791 through the Capuchin garden, the street honours Pierre Terrail de Bayard (1476-1524), born at the château Bayard in the commune of Pontcharra. It belongs to the antique dealers' district of Grenoble; at number 17, the laiterie Bayard, founded in 1931, sells milk from the farms of the Vercors.
summaries.Q118470124: First “rue Neuve des Capucins”, it became rue Saint-Vincent-de-Paul in 1837, then rue Voltaire in 1873. At number 17, the chapel of the Pénitents blancs, whose façade dates from 1657, holds 15th-century wooden stalls and serves as a place of worship for the Russian Orthodox parish of Grenoble.
summaries.Q109315611: Created by a resolution of the municipal council of 30 June 1902, this square marking the northern entrance to the city was called place de la Bastille, after the hill and the fort that overlook it. It was later renamed in tribute to Hubert Dubedout (1922-1986), mayor of Grenoble from 1965 to 1983.
summaries.Q111188742: Designed by Maurice Novarina to house about 2000 people, this village for the 1968 Winter Olympic Games was built from 1 April 1966 to November 1967: eleven four-storey buildings with façades mainly in wood and eight fifteen-storey towers. After the Games the district became residential and kept its name.
summaries.Q22979290: The city bought the land of the former Sainte-Claire convent in 1820; a market was held there from 1825, and its success led in 1874 to this building by Hector Riondel, inspired by the Baltard pavilions. The roof rests on cast-iron pillars, the brick walls not being load-bearing, and lions' heads decorate the corners.
summaries.Q2299298: The stadium cost about 200 trees in the parc Paul-Mistral: from November 2003 to February 2004, opponents who had come from all over Europe occupied the tops of the century-old trees, until they were removed by riot police in cherry pickers on 12 February 2004. Inaugurated in February 2008, the ground has 20,068 seats.
summaries.Q3146150: Inaugurated on 18 December 1967 in the run-up to the Winter Olympic Games, this 52.50-metre building replaces the hôtel de Lesdiguières, the town hall since 1719. Its tower, clad in a curtain wall by Jean Prouvé, weighs 8,000 tonnes and rests on a concrete beam with a span of 23 metres.
summaries.Q3268947: Heir to the Jesuit college founded in 1651, it is the oldest lycée in Grenoble: Stendhal and Champollion studied there. It keeps a solar clock of 1673 by Father Bonfa, an astronomer, a reflection dial fitted with two small fixed mirrors, listed as a historic monument in 1920.
summaries.Q3010215: In 1922 Félix Cartier-Millon announced to his wife the new name of his chocolate factory, Chocolats Marquise. She replied: “Who had that stupid idea?” He answered: “C'est moi”, it was me. Thus was born the Cémoi brand. Opened on rue Ampère in 1920, the factory was wound up on 21 July 1976; the site today houses offices.
summaries.Q1289: “At the end of every street, a mountain”, Stendhal said of this city surrounded by mountains. A Gaulish town named Cularo and then Gratianopolis, Grenoble became in the 11th century the capital of the Dauphiné, chosen by the counts of Albon. Its industrialisation began in the 18th century with glove-making and grew with hydroelectric power.
summaries.Q3329777: In 1989 the excavations for tramway line B brought to light a baptistery from the first Christian centuries: the route was shifted by a few metres and the ground excavated from 1991 to 1996. Housed in the episcopal palace, which sheltered 48 bishops until 1906, the museum opened on 18 September 1998.
summaries.Q821617: Born in 1966 in Stendhal's birthplace, rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau, the museum moved on 1 July 1994 to 14, rue Hébert, for the fiftieth anniversary of the liberation of Grenoble. Its collection exceeds 8,000 items; a relief model of ten square metres locates maquis, sabotage operations and parachute drops in the Isère.
